Abraomas Kulvietis
ah-brah'oh-mas kool-vye'tis
n. (c. 1510–1545; Lithuanian humanist and reformer, founder of the first higher school in Vilnius, driven into exile for the gospel)
Kulvietis, from the Lithuanian estate name Kulva; latinised as Culvensis, the man of Kulva.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Abraomas Kulvietis was a Lithuanian nobleman who studied at Cracow, Louvain, Leipzig and Wittenberg, took his doctorate in law at Siena, and came home in 1539 to open at Vilnius the first school of higher learning Lithuania had ever had. Some sixty sons of the nobility were taught there. He preached the gospel plainly and had Queen Bona's protection for a while; in 1542 Bishop Paulius Alsenietis moved against him, the school was shut, and Kulvietis fled to Prussia, where Duke Albert made him professor of Greek and Hebrew at Königsberg. He wrote his Confessio fidei there, the first Lithuanian Protestant confession, addressed to the queen who had failed to shield him. He came back to Lithuania in 1545 under a toleration edict and died within months, aged about thirty-five. The dictionary records him for the thing he would not do, which was be quiet: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a confession as the acknowledgment of a crime or of a belief, a formulary of articles of faith; exile as banishment, the state of being driven from one's country; and a testimony as a solemn declaration, in Scripture the divine law.

expand to see more

CONFESSION, n. [L. confessio.] The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something to one's disadvantage; a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.

EXILE, n. [L. exilium.] Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; the person banished.

TESTIMONY, n. [L. testimonium.] A solemn declaration or affirmation; in Scripture, the divine law, the two tables, the whole divine revelation.

SCATTER, v.t. To disperse; to dissipate; to separate and drive in different directions.

BOND, n. Anything that binds; a cord, a chain; an obligation; imprisonment, captivity.

Key Scripture

Psa 119:46 — "I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed."

Act 8:4 — "Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word."

2Ti 2:9 — "Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound."

Heb 11:38 — "(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth."

Modern Corruption

Lithuanian reformer who founded the first higher school in Vilnius in 1539, was driven out by the bishop in 1542, taught Greek and Hebrew at Königsberg, and wrote the first Lithuanian Protestant confession.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Kulvietis is sometimes claimed as a figure of national awakening and nothing else, a founder of Lithuanian letters whose religion was incidental to his patriotism. The order was the other way round. He learned Greek and Hebrew to read the Scriptures, taught them so that others could, and wrote his confession to a queen because he expected to be judged for what he believed and not for what he had built.

The principle to recover is that a scattering does not stop the word; it carries it. The pattern in Acts is not survival but advance: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). Paul in prison makes the same distinction between the preacher's circumstances and the word's liberty — “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9) — and the Psalm sets the posture for a man summoned before power with his Bible in his hand: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46). Hebrews gives the world's valuation of such men and corrects it in a parenthesis: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:)” (Heb 11:38).

Hebrew 'eduth (H5715), a testimony; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad.

Usage

"“I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46) — the Confessio fidei written at Königsberg for Queen Bona."

"“Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — the Vilnius school shut and its master in exile, 1542."

"“but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9) — professor of Greek and Hebrew in Prussia."
